speaker: KELLY AND DENA
words: [We are] on [the] CSU Stanislaus campus talking with uh Dr. Wayne Pierce and Dr. Ida Bowers. This is Kelly and I'm Dena and it is November the 9th of 2004.

speaker: DENA
words: And so um I guess we'll begin with our first question. Um Dr. Pierce, we would like to start with um just a brief overview of the processes that got the development of the bio-ag started.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Alright, we're missing one... a very important person from this. There were three of us that really uh were the main instigators of this this whole concept of bio-ag and an associated project called the Trans-California Pathway.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: That individual is Dr. David Gotelli and uh he retired in 1991 ... disability retirement... but he was one of the main instigators.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: He began uh getting interested in having an arboretum on campus in uh the 1980s.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: They had a project called [Heritage World?] which never came to fruition, but he was the... sort of the campus expert on developing an arboretum for that project.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: But when that failed, he still had the idea that we needed an arboretum on campus. And somehow the three of us got together talking about this in about uh 1985.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And I had an interest in native plants because of my teaching and [unclear] went out in the field and identified native plants. So the idea uh came about to have an arboretum involving primarily native plants.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And I think I was the one that came up with the idea of having a trans-California transit uh where you would have a strip of vegetation going from the corner of the

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: campus down toward the center and you'd have the different kinds of biomes that you have from the top of the Sierras down into the Central Valley, ending in the the valley grassland, which is

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: dominated by the Valley Oak. And at the same time, Ida had the idea that uh we needed a field site where students could go out and do experimental uh projects particularly uh in what some people call

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: biointensive uh gardening or agriculture. And subsequently... subsequently we came to call that permaculture but basically it's a... it's a... I could

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: explain that better later on but it uh that was a central theme of the the field site: a site where students and faculty could go out and do projects, do demonstration gardens. And so the two

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: were intimately linked for quite a long time. Whenever we would go before the campus planning committee or other bodies on campus, it was always the Trans-California Pathway and what we called

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: the field site. We early on we had a third component called theme plantings. The idea there was to have various kinds of plantings on campus ... we were going to have a a handicapped

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: uh garden planting uh for people who were blind, where they go up and smell different kinds of plants [and] uh a pollinarium which would attract different kinds of [insects,] particularly insect pollinators but possibly birds

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: as well. Interestingly, that has now come to fruition in our current bio-ag.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Uh, the theme planting idea sort of got lost along the way. We've we haven't abandoned it totally, but certainly our focus has been on these two projects, the Trans-California Pathway and and the

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: what we now have called the bio-ag field site. Uh from the beginning we we had the idea that both of these projects would would evolve slowly.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Uh and this was a a problem we had convincing administrators on campus that we should have such a project because the campus is accustomed to putting together a project and having it done

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: within a certain finite period of time. And we felt that if we were going to have a field site that could involve students for years to come, that both the projects needed to be evolved, not

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: just something that we plan and put in place and then it's more a static from there on. So that was our, our uh interest from the very beginning.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: I've gone to trouble to go through some of our old memos and so forth to get some of the important dates.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: We had this, this plan in our minds. Then we went before uh some campus administrators. Lee Cockrell [name/spelling uncertain] was an important individual. He was uh head of the facilities and planning at that time. And Carl Coffey was sort of second

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: in command in the Facilities [Planning and Operations] area. And when when Lloyd retired, Carl became sort of the lead person in terms of helping us out with both of these both of these projects. And we had an early

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: meeting and we developed a proposal with their help. First of all, we wanted to make sure that an arburetum was feasible. And we were told that uh something called an arboretum was

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: probably not feasible because the chancellor's office at that time had had some bad experiences with a couple bargainings (? unclear) in the system. And so we were going to have to be creative and come up with a name for it, that didn't... didn't immediately translate as an

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: arboretum. So that's how we came up with the Trans-California Pathway. Uh the field site was a little easier to sell because it did it was an area that we could just designate on campus and uh for students

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: to work. What became difficult over time was getting a site for that and that's sort of what this history is going to be about. [The] struggle with the three of us had initially and then since then Ida and I

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: had just getting a site designated for a field site for bio-ag.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And uh so we went through this in 1985 and 19.. 1986 discussions back and forth. We drafted an original proposal and uh this is something I have a copy of and we can meet with you for the campus archives.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: In June of 86, uh, David Gotelli and I wrote a memo to Don Bowers, who was then acting dean of ALS, and he requested information about potential uses of these sites.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: In order to... to justify something like this on the campus and to get it on the master plan, we had to demonstrate that there was actually going to be student involvement. And so we outlined several of the different kinds of projects that

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: uh we had in mind and again we have documentation that we can share and put in the archives. And then Don Bowers sent us uh response back. Let me just quote from part of what he said. "This proposal has

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: generated a great deal of interest and favorable response during this past year. My impression is that the campus strongly supports the project. Financial... Financing appears to be the most problematic concern."

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: [It] was and still is. [Chuckles all around.]

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Uh then in 19... December of 1986, David Gotelli uh drafted an update on the original proposal, adding things to it, clarifying things.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And there's a statement in there that I think reflects the philosophy that the three of us had about these two projects. So I'll just quote it. "It must be very clearly understood that the arburetum and field study site will be projects

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: with small beginnings that will evolve continually." And that's a philosophy that Ida and I have tried to carry on throughout this whole process. And you know, we met some resistance on this... continue to meet

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: some resistance... but I think we're we're gradually [unclear: riding them?] down. [Dr. Ida Bower echoes Dr. Pierce.]

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: In uh... From January to March 1987, the campus got our landscape architects involved in helping us draft uh a plan that could be then put on the campus master plan.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And this went through some iterations and uh they came up with a a draft of a plan.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And it took him took him the better part of that year to come up with the plan and also the cost for implementation of that plan.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And at that time the pathway would cost something in the neighborhood of $350,000 and the bio-ag site, called BAG now, uh roughly was $350,000 also.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: I was on sabbatical during uh much of 86 and into 87 and so I missed out on some of the work with the the

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: architects and if Ida has anything to add to what went on there, she's welcome to do it. Uh she and David went before the campus planning committee to to outline the

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: proposal both for the field site and the, and the pathway. And that's ultimately what led to this getting be placed on the campus... campus master plan.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: In uh... the period around 1988 - and I... I'm not sure about this date - they began to develop some parking lots on campus.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And one of the parking lots they developed was the one on Monte Vista - west of the science building - and they needed a place to put the soil. They dug down and they needed a place to put the soil.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And so that matched perfectly with our need for soil for the the pathway because our idea was to have two berns running parallel to Monta Vista down to the corner Monte Vista and Geer, uh which would kind of delineate the pathway.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: We'd have a stream coming down through the middle of that. That would ultimately connect with a pond located on the field side.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: That was our original concept. If you look at this, I don't know if you can see this drafting here from the campus. In fact, this is probably from the architects. Here is uh, the current science building approximately here.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: [Dr. Pierce is pointing to a set of blueprints on easel.] Here was the original site of the the pond, which now is called Willow Lake. And then the field site was basically this area here. Then we had, it's not showing here, but then we had a stream

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: connecting the pathway project which stretched down along here and all the way down along the frontage there, to the corner where the where the fountain's located [at the time of this interview the campus marker on the southeast corner of the campus had an operating fountain instead of a flower/plant bed].

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And so they they dug up the parking lot and they made the two... two berns. They also dug out this area here, uh as a.... as our pond, hoping that uh this

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: could be lined and would hold water. Well, shortly thereafter, we had uh several floods on campus or two floods on campus where several parking lots were flooded. People had water in their cars.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And during that entire time, this thing didn't didn't hold a drop of water. And so the facilities people began to look at some soil maps and they discovered that this was a location of an underground.... old underground stream.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And so basically it was a sand bed. So the water would go in there and percolate down. And so obviously that site probably was not going to be work... not going to work even if we lined it with... with clay, which was what our original plan was.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Once the the berns were put in place in 1988, December 1988, we planted our first Valley Oaks. Uh that's part of the

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Trans-California Pathway and that's situated [unclear] here. And if you go down into that part of the campus, you'll see some Valley Oak trees that are now 20, 30 ft high.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: We planted the first ones in 88. The second planting was in uh spring of ...uh 1990.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And those trees were donated by then Senator Dan McCorquodale. He was going statewide doing a project trying to replant oaks, not just Valley Oaks, but all native oaks in California.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: So he had some, some Valley Oaks and he uh added... gave us some additional trees to plant and we lost quite a few of the first planting. So that worked out very nicely.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And so that was the beginning of the pathway and that's pretty much where the pathway sits today. Uh, we still have the berns. We still have the plan. It's still on the master plan. Uh, I went before the committee, the planning

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: committee just this last spring to to go after some funding for this. And so it's, it's still there. We had a masters student do a project planning one of the one of the, the biomes within this pathway um way back in the beginning of this process.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: But since that first planting and the subsequent watering that several of us did to keep the plants alive for two or three years, most of our attention has been focused on the field site.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And we felt it was important that we concentrate on one of these two projects.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And once we got it in place, and by that I mean fencing, uh, a building that we could call an office and a meeting place, uh,

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: a storage shed and infrastructure, power, and water... underground. Once we got that in place, then we felt we had a

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: site where students could could do some work. And this took us up into the mid '90s. We had finally had a meeting uh with campus planning committee again in

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: 1996 and uh took a proposal called the bio-ag center (that time called the bio-ag center) and took it to the campus planning committee.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And at that point uh after several other meetings of various campus administrators including uh deans and vice presidents and [unclear] presidents.
Uh, we got approval for the current site where bio-ag is today. Part of that approval included uh fencing of the site that was adjacent to a pond which had been dug, uh

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: called Willow Lake, adjacent to the field site and we now consider to be part of bio-ag.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Uh that pond was put there like all the other ponds in campus to to handle runoff that occurs from our parking lots primarily during heavy rain. They had learned that we started putting in all these parking lots and they didn't have

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: any place for the water to go. The campus is under uh, uh guidelines from the state and the city that [say] we have to impound our runoff

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: water for a period of time after a storm before it can be put into the local... local irrigation districts and so forth.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Originally they had in mind some little ponds like this. Well, they did some computations and figured out that if you take a whole bunch of these little ponds to capture the water. And so what we've ended up with

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: are all these different uh ponds on campus which they decided rather than having dry as was on the original master plan, they decided well if we're going to have them, let's... let's have them be something that's beautiful to look at the whole year.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And so that's how they evolved. If you look at some of the things that they've done with those ponds, some of the the ideas that they gleaned are things that we had planned for the path, the stream... running stream, the rocks.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: When you look at some of the rockways that go into some of the ponds that went over by the classroom building, uh you see some of the ideas that that we had early on in the development of the pathway project.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: So that's uh that's about where we finally got the site. We got it fenced. Uh, we were the beneficiary of the donation of the dome building that you see. Often we call [it] the geodome, which we use as an office and meeting place.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: It's got a kitchen. It's got computer uh stations hooked up to the internet and uh we sub.. subsequently

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: uh this last I guess a year ago, two years ago, we had the composting toilets put in as a demonstration project for sustainable.... One of our major concepts

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: of this whole bio-ag site area was to have demonstration projects in this various kinds of sustainability: biointensive gardening, permaculture, solar applications,

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: composting toilets, and so forth. And uh so they built the composting toilets with a storage shed, which was our next biggest need because we had no place to store our tools. And so if we left tools out there, there's a pretty good

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: chance next time we came back, they wouldn't be there. And so now we have security on that. We have place where we can store seeds and those kind of items.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: And so now we really have a working uh working site. Prior to all this, Ida's students in particular used this site for various kinds of projects. And she

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: can tell you a little more about that. Basically from, I think almost the mid 1980s onward with a break from the dig Willow Lake and to cover up the bio-ag area with

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: some of that soil - we had continuous student projects out there on that site even before it was fenced. And I'll ,I'll there with the the brief history of how we got to be where we are are at this point in time.

speaker: KELLY
words: All right. You've kind of talked about some different ideas and themes that have come into it. What do you see [pointing to one professor] in in your opinion [pointing to other professor] and in your opinion as being the main focus... main focus of the bio-ag?

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: Our concept of the bio-ag from the very beginning was that it would be a site on campus where students from many

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: different disciplines could gather and work in teams on anything having to do with human relationships to the land... the use of... But we wanted it to always have a

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: sustainable focus and an environmentally healthy focus, an ecologically sound focus.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: So um I I want you to realize that from the very beginning I have these two and eventually they'll end up in the archives. Um our students were working along. They got excited about these

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: ideas and they began to to uh design projects and um ideas for... like here's one for a solar greenhouse and workshop... and they have designs for it and

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: sketches that they've done and all kinds of things like that. Um, our our idea was always that it should be that it should be open to any discipline.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: For example, um I've been trying over all of these years to get someone from music interested in designing a garden where it's a musical garden where the

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: plants have different structures and as the wind blows through they make different sounds. We've also wished that someone would design um a garden that was specifically for people who are

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: blind where they could um... where it's tactile. They could have sticky plants and soft plants and boring plants and all kinds of things that children could experience. We we have so many ideas for

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: theme gardens that go along with that. But I think the most important... most important themes from the very beginning were uh cooperation across disciplines,

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: involving lots of students and faculty, and um always following the principles of ecologically sound sustainable use of the land. And if we're going to do that,

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: it has to be flexible. It has to be able to evolve over time, not build a garden site, plant all the gardens, then it's always the same all the time. And that

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: has been actually, I think, one of our most difficult concepts to get across to people on the campus. They expect to see the entire bio-ag planted and always

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: have gardens and always have the same thing. And we're out there experimenting and trying different things. One of our major themes also is you know the Central Valley is one of the most most diver... ethnically diverse areas on the face of the earth.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: It is like a United Nations on the land. We have so many different ethnic groups. Each ethnic group comes with their own knowledge of plants and animals and their own

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: relationships and belief systems as they interact with those. One of our themes in the bio-ag is to... to um demonstrate ethnobbotany and ethnoecology...

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: to have um garden sites where we can demonstrate what does a Mexican home garden look like? What does an African home garden look like?

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: What are the common plants? How about Hmong medicinal plants? Uh what about, um any of the other groups that we have?

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: Can we do representative gardens from those different ethnic groups? Um, so ethnobotony, ethnoecology, sustainability, multi-disiplinary work, those have all been what we're working on.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: It has been frustrating for us because for a long time we worked out there in that... we... it was... I don't like the term "we" but everyone knows what we're talking about.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Native area.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: Native area. Um, and our students would go out and they do double digging, which is a basic part of biointensive agriculture, and then plant, demonstrate

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: companion planting, and we'd have different kinds of beds out there in the midst of this field that was otherwise tumble weeds and things like that. Um we did that for a number of years, waiting for the site to be identified.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: And then the site was identified and the soil was spread on it. Unfortunately, a lot of that soil was greatly compacted by the heavy machinery which was used to dig

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: the pond and then later on to put up the structures that are out there, set up the fence, put in the piping. And we just [got] going on something... We didn't really get into the site inside the fence until

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: about the year 2000. And so, while the dream has been there for a long time, being able to actually have it on site and protect it and so on, has only been very recently.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: And then in... in I think it was 2002, they started to build the storage room, which means you bring out heavy equipment again. They did that in the winter, so

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: it was muddy and and really quite a sight. Um, [it is] difficult to sustain projects to have the continuity you need to sustain projects out there. So, that has

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: been frustrating because some people on the campus will say, well, my goodness, this has been in the works since it was approved by facilities planning... [in] 1996.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: Why isn't it there? And we've been out there pulling up the star vessel and trying to get the beds going and then they come in with the equipment and and dig deep these big trenches for pipes and electrical conduits and so on. So

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: it's coming. It's coming. It just takes time.

speaker: DENA
words: So that is a process, I'll tell you. Um back to... um I have a question regarding fundraising, because obviously funds are a major issue, which uh Dr. Pierce um elaborated on. I would just like to ask um... Is there...

speaker: DENA
words: Who was in charge of seeking or handling any type of donations other than the actual building itself? Um and also was there ever any kind of fundraising um ideas thought about or anything attempted yet? [chuckles]

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: We talked about a lot of things, but none of us had very much time. We were we we've we have our classes on top of this and our work to do and um it's hard for us to go out and raise funds.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: We've requested again and again, of course, funds, coordinators, funds for a coordinator. That's our biggest problem. There's no funding for graduate students or for students or for a coordinator to coordinate the work out there.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: And so it has been very difficult for us to have that kind of continuity. Um so there has not been a lot of fundraising. Sandell Davidson who... Sandell

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: McLaughlin - who I believe will be interviewed later on and be a part of this series - uh did some fundraising when she was a graduate student here and got a donation of about

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: $800 from the community that is still available and we're slowly spending it to buy seeds and plants and once in a while a tool or something. Most of the

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: tools out there have been donated by either faculty or students. Most of the things we use have been donated um because we're afraid we won't get any more funding. We're very careful about spending that. So it's just doled out carefully.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: Um, so we haven't done a lot with... Our dream was that once the gardens began to produce, um, we could have a a weekly sale, plant

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: sale, vegetable sale, all of that on the campus and that would be an a source of funding for the bio-ag, but we we don't have it there yet. In fact, about two years ago, the sociology club and the

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: Hunger Network started a project out there called Harvest for the Homeless. So, most of any yields we have, whether it's fruit or vegetables or whatever it is from the bio-ag goes to a site in Turlock that feeds the homeless.

speaker: DENA
words: So, which... which is wonderful.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: Yeah, we're very happy about that. Very good.

speaker: DENA
words: Talking about the community, what connections has the bio-ag project made um uh, with the local agra business um to possibly inquire about uh methods of land preservation, uh pesticide usage, uh [and/or] any other types of ecological concerns with the land.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Well, I think our number one priority has always been to the extent possible, the non-use of pesticides.

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: That's in keeping with our idea of sustainability. Uh we've had to back down on that a little bit this year because of the problem with the cattails in Willow Lake which is... we

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: consider part of part of Bio-ag. We tried doing mechanical removal last year and that was less than successful. And so the the campus powers

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: that be are trying to convince us that we at least need to attempt a chemical means of uh letting the.. the pond of some of the... of the cattails because it's... it's becoming in...

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: uh surrounded by them and more importantly they're getting into [unclear] in the pond. So, uh, they have sprayed a chemical for the first time and we'll

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: see how this see how this... this works. It's... it's not it's a thing that's not going to be successful with just one spraying. I have a feeling we're going to have to come back probably year after year at least for a while

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: ...spraying. Um, what was the rest of your question?

speaker: DENA
words: Well, I was just curious uh about uh any connections that you might have tried to make with any local agra business, uh bringing that um into uh the bio-ag with the different types of methods that they might use for uh preservation of the land or?

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: Well, we've had a donation of fruit trees by Dave Wilson Nursery... very important donation. And uh the idea there was to put them along our fence line them so you don't take much space. One of the the ideas for this uh area is to

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: demonstrate ways of planting things in small spaces. So, raised beds um, planting fruit trees along the fence, and u and so we had a a nice donation of

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: fruit trees several years ago, right after it opened, by David Wilson Nursery. And our original thought at the time was that we would uh bring in trees year after year

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: and we haven't gone back and planted a second plant. We planted a tree one fence post and we left the gap, planted a different variety of fruit tree. The idea was to come back and plant other varieties of the same plant in

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: subsequent years. We've had so much turmoil out there in terms of activity of construction and so forth that we've really put that in advance until things have finally stabilized. And we think for the first time, we have a stable

speaker: DR. WAYNE PIERCE
words: site. There's no longer going to be any any serious dating and so forth taking place. And now we can begin to have some more permanent kinds of kinds of demonstration plots.

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: And in fact, one of the students this year is working on a design... to and she's going back to Dave Wilson Nursery to do this um because they said they would

speaker: DR. IDA BOWERS
words: donate the trees. Um the person who arranged that at Dave Wilson Nursery, Ed Laivo is the educational person at the Wilson Nursery and he has always had this concept of... and in fact he has it in
